metadata.title: The Efficiency of Secondary Schools in an International Perspective (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 microdata merged from student and school questionnaires and constructs school-level inputs/outputs by aggregating student-level measures to the school level. For school-level variable construction, the authors explicitly state that they use student weights W_FSTUWT when building school averages (e.g., ESCS at school level). The efficiency scores are then computed at the school level using Data Envelopment Analysis with bootstrap bias correction, and a second-stage Tobit regression relates bootstrapped, bias-corrected efficiency to school-level covariates. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) for the second-stage regression, so uncertainty quantification relies on the DEA bootstrap rather than survey replicate methods.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an official IEA/OECD technical report or assessment framework. It describes sampling, scaling, and instrument design rather than student-level predictive modeling. Plausible values are therefore not applicable to the document's primary analytic purpose; any missing-data discussion refers to fieldwork or scaling procedures, not a single ML imputation strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PISA 2012 school-level data for 30 countries: all OECD countries including Singapore and excluding Chile, Greece, Hungary, Mexico, and Turkey. The analytic unit is schools (not students): the baseline DEA uses 3 inputs (ESCS, StRatio, Computer_n) and 2 outputs (pv1math, pv1read) constructed as school averages. Schools are excluded if at least one of these five indicators is missing, yielding 8,640 schools in the final sample (Table 1). For the second-stage regression, the same school sample is used and additional covariates are included; the authors note that some countries (AUT, DNK, POL) are excluded from certain second-stage models due to missing data or multicollinearity.

data.outcome_summary: The paper derives school efficiency measures using PISA 2012 data for 8,640 schools across 30 OECD countries (excluding Chile, Greece, Hungary, Mexico, and Turkey). Inputs are school-average ESCS, the inverse student-teacher ratio, and computers per student; outputs are mathematics and reading achievement based on PISA plausible values, with the baseline using pv1 and robustness checks using other PVs. Efficiency is estimated via bootstrap bias-corrected Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) with an international frontier benchmark, then related to school-level factors using a second-stage Tobit regression (and quantile regression) with country fixed effects. The study estimates that, holding inputs constant, schools could raise achievement by about 27% on average using more efficient input-output combinations, with substantial within- and between-country variation. It finds no evidence of a trade-off between efficiency and inclusion: higher efficiency aligns with a lower proportion of students below proficiency Level 2 and better student attitudes (e.g., lower truancy). Limitations include the proxy nature of school-level efficiency (PISA is not designed for school representativeness) and the correlational interpretation of second-stage associations.
